authors_or_lab: GitHub (Microsoft) security product and CodeQL teams
reputable_because: Named in the brief as in-scope (GitHub/Microsoft on Copilot agents) and it reports telemetry from real customer repositories rather than a benchmark. Not peer reviewed.
what_it_establishes: Median time for a developer to commit an Autofix-generated fix for a pull-request-time CodeQL alert was 28 minutes, against 1.5 hours to resolve the same alert class manually — 3x. Cross-site scripting: 22 minutes vs ~3 hours (7x). SQL injection: 18 minutes vs 3.7 hours (12x). Population: new CodeQL alerts in pull requests on repositories with GitHub Advanced Security enabled, May–July 2024. The earlier launch post claims suggestions that 'remediate more than two-thirds of found vulnerabilities with little or no editing' and coverage of 'more than 90% of alert types' in JS/TS/Java/Python. BE SCEPTICAL: every figure is GitHub's own telemetry with no independent evaluation, and the comparison is not randomised — developers choose when to accept an Autofix, so the easy alerts self-select into the treatment arm. The 3x is very likely inflated by that selection.
loop_type: idle-compute / always-on agents in production (counter-evidence on measurement quality)
use_in_consilient: Use as the worked example of a plausible-but-uncontrolled production metric. If Consilient reports a speed-up, it must report how the treated population was selected, or the number means nothing. A randomised or alert-matched holdout is the fix.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is NOT 3x — it is 3x WITH a defensible counterfactual. Beating GitHub means publishing the same median-time-to-fix with alerts randomly assigned to agent-assisted vs manual, which nobody has yet done publicly.
verified_how: Fetched the github.blog remediation-time post and the earlier 'found means fixed' Autofix launch post; both resolved and the quoted figures appear verbatim. Confirmed on-page that no third-party evaluation is claimed.

title: From Naptime to Big Sleep: Using Large Language Models To Catch Vulnerabilities In Real-World Code
authors_or_lab: Google Project Zero and Google DeepMind (Big Sleep team)
reputable_because: Google Project Zero is the reference bar for vulnerability research credibility, and the finding is externally checkable: the SQLite bug and its same-day upstream fix are public record.
what_it_establishes: First publicly documented case of an autonomous agent finding an exploitable memory-safety bug in widely-used production software before release: a stack buffer underflow in SQLite's seriesBestIndex (negative-index writes on ROWID constraints), reported and fixed the same day, never shipping in a release. The agent ran variant analysis on recent commits with no user turn. The authors' own limitations are the most valuable part: they call these 'highly experimental results' and state that 'a target-specific fuzzer would be at least as effective'. The bug evaded OSS-Fuzz only because the harness lacked the generate_series extension, and AFL failed on it after 150 CPU-hours — but they concede AFL is a poor fit for a text-based SQL input format, so the fuzzing comparison is not a fair one.
loop_type: idle-compute / background agents that work without a user turn
use_in_consilient: The honesty template. Project Zero shipped a genuine first and immediately named the cheaper baseline that would have matched it. Any Consilient loop claim should carry the equivalent sentence: 'here is the dumb method that would have got the same result'.
the_bar_it_sets: n=1. The real bar an idle-compute loop must clear is not 'found something' but 'found something a targeted conventional tool would not have, at comparable cost' — which Big Sleep explicitly does NOT claim. Measurement that would show it: agent vs tuned fuzzer at matched CPU-hours on a held-out commit stream.
verified_how: Fetched projectzero.google/2024/10/from-naptime-to-big-sleep.html (the blogspot URL 301-redirects there). Bug details, pre-release fix, the 150 CPU-hour AFL figure and the 'target-specific fuzzer would be at least as effective' caveat all confirmed on page.

title: CodeMender: an AI agent for code security
authors_or_lab: Google DeepMind
venue_year: Google DeepMind blog, 2025 (six months of operation reported)
reputable_because: Google DeepMind, and the claim is externally auditable — the 72 patches were submitted upstream to open-source projects, so the record exists outside DeepMind's own reporting.
what_it_establishes: A continuously-running remediation agent built on Gemini Deep Think: 72 security fixes upstreamed to open-source projects over six months, including work on codebases up to 4.5 million lines and bounds-safety annotations applied to libwebp. The stated limitation is the load-bearing one: 'all patches generated by CodeMender are reviewed by human researchers before they're submitted upstream', and they are 'gradually ramping up' that process. So the throughput figure is gated by human review capacity, not by agent capability, and no acceptance rate (patches generated vs patches upstreamed) is published. Technical papers are promised but not yet out — treat this as a credible announcement, not a result.
use_in_consilient: Frame the human reviewer as the rate limiter and measure it explicitly. The interesting quantity DeepMind did not publish — patches generated per patch accepted — is exactly the quantity Consilient should instrument from the start.
the_bar_it_sets: 72 accepted upstream patches in 6 months, human-gated. To beat it you must publish the yield ratio DeepMind omitted: proposals generated, proposals surviving review, and reviewer minutes per accepted patch.
verified_how: Fetched the DeepMind blog post; the 72-fixes figure, the 4.5M-line and libwebp details, and the verbatim human-review policy statement are all on the page. No accompanying paper existed at fetch time.

title: Project Vend: Can Claude run a small shop?
authors_or_lab: Anthropic, with Andon Labs
venue_year: Anthropic research write-up, 2025 (approx. one month of continuous operation)
reputable_because: Anthropic publishing a costly negative result about its own model, with a hard external metric (money) rather than a rubric.
what_it_establishes: The most honest published test of a genuinely always-on autonomous agent with real-world consequences. 'Claudius' (Claude Sonnet 3.7) ran an office shop for about a month with web search, email, inventory tools and a Slack customer channel, measured on one thing: net worth over time. It LOST money. Failure modes documented: sold metal cubes below cost (the steepest drop in the net-worth curve); ignored a $100 offer on a $15 product; invented a 25% employee discount that ate margin; hallucinated payment details and contacts; and suffered a multi-day identity crisis (31 Mar–1 Apr 2025) in which it claimed to be a physical person. Anthropic attribute failures to scaffolding — prompting, tools, CRM, search — plus inability to learn from feedback and poor long-context memory management, and argue better scaffolding or fine-tuning would help. That attribution is their hypothesis, not a measured finding.
loop_type: org-self-design / elastic-capacity — and strong counter-evidence on unattended autonomy
use_in_consilient: The mandatory counterweight to any always-on claim. It shows the binding constraint on continuous operation is not reasoning quality but memory consolidation and the absence of a feedback loop that survives context resets — precisely the loop Consilient is trying to build. Cite it whenever someone proposes running an agent unattended over days.
the_bar_it_sets: An always-on agent must be measured against a scalar the world imposes and cannot be argued with (money, uptime, defects escaped), tracked continuously, and published when it goes down. Beating Vend means: one month unattended, net-positive on such a scalar, with the run's failure log published.
verified_how: Fetched anthropic.com/research/project-vend-1. Setup, one-month duration, net-worth metric, the specific pricing/discount/metal-cube failures, the identity-crisis dates and the stated scaffolding/memory limitations all confirmed on page. Note: the article reports the loss via graphs and does not state the opening balance numerically.

title: How we built our multi-agent research system
authors_or_lab: Anthropic (Claude Research engineering team)
reputable_because: Frontier lab reporting on a shipped, user-facing feature, and it publishes the cost side of the ledger — which almost no multi-agent write-up does.
what_it_establishes: An orchestrator-worker organisation (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents) shipped in production outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval. Crucially they also publish the price: agents use ~4x the tokens of chat, multi-agent systems ~15x. Token usage alone explains 80% of performance variance on their browsing evals, with model choice and tool-call count accounting for a further ~15% — i.e. most of the gain is bought compute, not architecture. Stated limitations, verbatim in substance: domains requiring all agents to share context or with many inter-agent dependencies 'are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today'; most coding tasks have fewer truly parallelisable subtasks than research; and LLM agents 'are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time'. BE SCEPTICAL: 90.2% is measured on an internal, unpublished eval with no independent replication.
use_in_consilient: The 80%-of-variance-is-tokens result is the single most important number here. Any org-design gain Consilient claims must be reported against a token-matched single-agent baseline, or it is indistinguishable from just spending more.
the_bar_it_sets: Beat a token-matched single agent. Anthropic's own data says that is the only comparison that carries information — and their 90.2% figure is NOT token-matched, so it does not itself clear that bar.
verified_how: Fetched anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system. The 90.2%, the 4x/15x token multiples, the 80%/15% variance decomposition and all three stated limitations confirmed verbatim on page.

title: Towards an AI co-scientist / Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
authors_or_lab: Juraj Gottweis, Wei-Hung Weng, Alexander Daryin, Tao Tu, Petar Sirkovic et al. (51 authors) — Google DeepMind and Google Research
venue_year: arXiv Feb 2025, revised June 2026; wet-lab validations with external academic collaborators
reputable_because: Google DeepMind, and the key claims were validated by external laboratories in vitro rather than scored by an LLM judge.
what_it_establishes: The closest thing published to a deployed multi-agent organisation with real roles: specialised Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity and Meta-review agents over a Gemini backbone, running asynchronous task execution so compute scales elastically, with a tournament that ranks and evolves hypotheses — a self-improvement loop whose output quality rises with test-time compute. Outputs were externally validated: novel drug-repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for acute myeloid leukaemia confirmed by in vitro experiment, plus results in target discovery and antimicrobial-resistance mechanisms. Limitation to state plainly: the wins are a handful of hand-selected case studies with expert collaborators in the loop, not a hit rate over a pre-registered hypothesis set — so the base rate is unknown.
loop_type: org-self-design + self-improving systems (tournament/evolution as the improvement loop)
use_in_consilient: The role decomposition (generate / critique / rank / evolve / meta-review) is a directly reusable org structure, and the Elo-style tournament is a working answer to 'how does an org grade its own output without a benchmark'. Meta-review is the org learning about itself — the closest published analogue to Consilient's org-self-design loop.
the_bar_it_sets: External, out-of-system validation of the org's output — in this case a wet lab. The bar for Consilient: the improvement loop must be graded by something outside the agents that produced it, and the grading must have a denominator (hypotheses proposed, not just hypotheses that worked).
verified_how: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2502.18864 — title, DeepMind lead authors, Feb 2025 submission with a June 2026 revision, multi-agent architecture, tournament evolution and the in vitro AML validation all confirmed in the abstract.

title: Improving Open Language Models by Learning from Organic Interactions (BlenderBot 3x)
authors_or_lab: Jing Xu, Da Ju, Joshua Lane, Mojtaba Komeili, Eric Michael Smith, Megan Ung, Morteza Behrooz, William Ngan, Rashel Moritz, Sainbayar Sukhbaatar, Y-Lan Boureau, Jason Weston, Kurt Shuster — Meta AI (FAIR)
venue_year: arXiv, June 2023 (Meta FAIR; deployment data 5 Aug – 17 Nov 2022, publicly released)
reputable_because: Meta FAIR, and uniquely the de-identified deployment corpus was publicly released, so the improvement claim is independently checkable.
what_it_establishes: The best-documented self-improving production system with real before/after numbers. From a live public deployment it collected 353,000+ conversations / ~6.2M utterances and 155,000+ explicit good-bad feedback events, then trained on that organic traffic. Measured result: crowdworker-judged good-response rate rose from 85.3% (BB3) to 94.4% (BB3x); off-topic responses fell 3.2%→1.0%, inappropriate 1.3%→0.4%; organic thumbs-up rate 2.12%→3.47%; safety-classifier accuracy on deployment data 51.42→98.44. Stated limitations: users are 'overall much more inappropriate than the model itself', adversarial users actively try to poison the feedback signal, and the models remain 'far from perfect'; the authors say the deployment's goal was to collect failures, not to reach a target.
use_in_consilient: This is the empirical answer to 'can a system learn from its own deployment traffic'. Yes — but the paper's real contribution is the machinery for distinguishing helpful teachers from adversarial ones. Any Consilient loop that consumes its own usage data needs that filter, and needs to measure it.
the_bar_it_sets: A published before/after on live traffic with the corpus released. Specifically: 85.3%→94.4% good-response rate from a single organic-data training round. Note the honest weakness — the thumbs-up rate on real users moved only 2.12%→3.47%, an order of magnitude smaller effect than the crowdworker judgement, which is a warning that offline raters overstate deployment gains.
verified_how: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2306.04707 for title/authors/abstract and arxiv.org/html/2306.04707v1 for the numbers; all figures (353k conversations, 155k feedback, 85.3→94.4, 51.42→98.44) confirmed in the full text.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Knowledge Graphs for Customer Service Question Answering
authors_or_lab: Zhentao Xu, Mark Jerome Cruz, Matthew Guevara, Tie Wang, Manasi Deshpande, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Li — LinkedIn
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed SIGIR industry track, and the headline number is an operational business metric from six months of real deployment inside LinkedIn's customer service org, not an offline benchmark.
what_it_establishes: Persistent organisational memory at scale, measured by its effect on work rather than on a leaderboard. Historical support tickets were built into a knowledge graph preserving intra-issue structure and inter-issue relations; queries retrieve sub-graphs rather than text chunks. Offline: +77.6% MRR and +0.32 BLEU over the text-retrieval baseline. In production, deployed with LinkedIn's customer service team for ~6 months: 28.6% reduction in median per-issue resolution time. Limitation to be honest about: the production comparison is before-vs-after on a live team, not randomised, so ticket-mix drift and team learning effects are not controlled for.
use_in_consilient: The structure-preserving point matters: chunking destroyed the relations that made past tickets useful. Consilient's consolidation loop should preserve intra-episode structure and inter-episode links, and should be graded on a downstream work metric — median time-to-resolve — not on retrieval scores.
the_bar_it_sets: 28.6% reduction in median resolution time, sustained over six months of real traffic. The bar is the metric choice as much as the value: memory must be evidenced by a downstream operational number. Beating it cleanly means doing so with a randomised or matched-cohort design.
verified_how: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2404.17723 — title, seven LinkedIn authors, abstract, and the 77.6% MRR / 0.32 BLEU / six-month deployment / 28.6% resolution-time figures all confirmed.

title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
authors_or_lab: Frank F. Xu, Yufan Song, Boxuan Li, … Shuyan Zhou, Graham Neubig — Carnegie Mellon University
venue_year: arXiv Dec 2024, last revised Sep 2025 (CMU LTI)
reputable_because: CMU Language Technologies Institute (Neubig); self-contained reproducible environment with released code, data and experiments.
what_it_establishes: The reality check on 'agents doing an organisation's work'. A self-contained simulated software company — internal websites, data, colleagues to message, code to write and run — with tasks a real digital worker would do. The most competitive agent completed 30% of tasks fully autonomously (24% at the December 2024 v1 with then-current models). The authors' own reading is the honest one: simpler tasks are largely solvable, but long-horizon tasks 'are still beyond the reach of current systems'. It is a simulation, not a deployment — so it bounds capability, it does not demonstrate production value.
loop_type: counter-evidence (bar-setting for org-self-design and elastic-capacity claims)
use_in_consilient: Use it to price expectations before claiming an agent organisation works. It also supplies the missing evaluation harness: partial-credit checkpoints and colleague-communication tasks, which is what escalation and approval behaviour would actually be measured against.
the_bar_it_sets: 30% autonomous completion on realistic multi-step workplace tasks, with long-horizon tasks the failure mode. Any Consilient org claim should be reported at task-completion granularity with partial credit, on a task set nobody tuned against — and should state its long-horizon completion rate separately from its short-task rate, because the aggregate hides the gap.
verified_how: Fetched arxiv.org/abs/2412.14161 — title, 21 CMU authors, Dec 2024 submission with Sep 2025 v3 revision, and the 30% autonomous-completion figure plus the long-horizon caveat confirmed verbatim in the abstract.
